scenes.visual: Title card 'One Flow, Two Pressures' over a simple cartoon heart split down the middle, right half BLUE, left half RED. COLOUR MAP for the whole film (and the second film): oxygen-poor blood BLUE; oxygen-rich blood RED; ventricles drawn as GOLD lifts (elevator platforms); pressure drawn as HEIGHT on a vertical axis labelled 'pressure (schematic)'; resistance drawn as a narrowing GREY channel (narrowness, not branching, shows resistance; dot throughput stays equal in steady state). All shapes are labelled 'schematic'. No molecules.

scenes.tts: Both sides of your heart pump the same flow of blood every minute. So why does the left side push so much harder than the right?
scenes.visual: The split cartoon heart beats. Two identical flow counters, one under each half, labelled 'flow, right side' and 'flow, left side', tick upward at exactly the same rate. Above each half a pressure bar rises with each beat: the left (RED) bar shoots several times higher than the right (BLUE) bar. A large '?' appears between the bars.
scenes.narration: Both sides of your heart pump the same flow of blood every minute. So why does the left side push so much harder than the right?

scenes.tts: Start with flow. Flow is the volume of blood moved each minute. One ventricle's flow is its heart rate times its stroke volume, the blood it ejects with each beat.
scenes.visual: A single ventricle drawn as a cup squeezes out a scoop of blood each beat into a measuring jug; a metronome beside it ticks. On screen, building term by term: 'flow = heart rate × stroke volume'. Label the scoop 'stroke volume', the metronome 'heart rate', the jug 'flow (litres per minute)'.
scenes.narration: Start with flow. Flow is the volume of blood moved each minute. One ventricle's flow is its heart rate times its stroke volume, the blood it ejects with each beat.

scenes.tts: Now follow the loop. The right ventricle sends oxygen-poor blood through the lungs. It comes back oxygen-rich to the left side, which sends it through the body.
scenes.visual: A flat figure-eight loop. Right ventricle (GOLD, labelled 'right ventricle') pushes BLUE dots up through a box labelled 'lungs'; dots turn RED inside the lungs, return to the 'left ventricle' (GOLD), which pushes them round a larger box labelled 'body'; dots turn BLUE there and return to the right side.
scenes.narration: Now follow the loop. The right ventricle sends oxygen-poor blood through the lungs. It comes back oxygen-rich to the left side, which sends it through the body.

scenes.tts: The two sides pump one after the other, in series. Blood leaving one side must pass through the other before it comes back. So over time, their average flows must be equal.
scenes.visual: The dots stream round the figure-eight. A bead marked 'one drop' completes a full lap, visiting both ventricles in turn. The two flow counters from the opening return beside each ventricle, ticking in lockstep. Label 'in series: average flows equal'. On screen only: 'about 5 L per min each'.
scenes.narration: The two sides pump one after the other, in series. Blood leaving one side must pass through the other before it comes back. So over time, their average flows must be equal.

scenes.tts: Now draw pressure as height. Each ventricle is a lift that raises blood up. Then blood rolls downhill through its circuit, from high pressure to low.
scenes.visual: The figure-eight flattens and unrolls into a side-on landscape. The vertical axis is labelled 'pressure (schematic)'. Each GOLD ventricle becomes a lift platform raising dots; after each lift, the dots roll down a slope (the circuit) to the foot of the next lift. Labels: 'lift = ventricle', 'slope = circuit'.
scenes.narration: Now draw pressure as height. Each ventricle is a lift that raises blood up. Then blood rolls downhill through its circuit, from high pressure to low.

scenes.tts: Some circuits are harder to push through. Narrow vessels resist the flow, like a narrow pipe. Call that resistance. The pressure drop across a circuit equals the flow times its resistance.
scenes.visual: A slope is shown as a GREY channel that narrows along its length. Dots pass through at the same steady rate as before (no crowding or pile-up); the slope's height falls steeply where the channel is narrow. On screen, building: 'pressure drop = flow × resistance'. A bracket from the top to the bottom of the slope is labelled 'pressure drop (mean in − mean out)'. Do not draw extra parallel branches as the cause of resistance.
scenes.narration: Some circuits are harder to push through. Narrow vessels resist the flow, like a narrow pipe. Call that resistance. The pressure drop across a circuit equals the flow times its resistance.

scenes.tts: The lungs resist the flow only a little. So the right ventricle needs only a small lift to drive the whole flow through them.
scenes.visual: The lung slope: short, wide GREY channel, gentle. The right ventricle's GOLD lift rises a small step; BLUE dots roll easily down the short slope, turning RED. The flow counter ticks at its usual rate. Label 'lungs: low resistance, small drop'.
scenes.narration: The lungs resist the flow only a little. So the right ventricle needs only a small lift to drive the whole flow through them.

scenes.tts: The body's circuit resists far more. So the left ventricle must lift the same flow much higher, to drive it down that long, narrow slope.
scenes.visual: The body slope: long, steep, narrow GREY channel. The left ventricle's GOLD lift climbs high above the right one; RED dots roll down the long slope at the same steady rate, turning BLUE. The flow counter beside it ticks at exactly the same rate as the lung side. Label 'body: high resistance, big drop'. No numbers for the ratio.
scenes.narration: The body's circuit resists far more. So the left ventricle must lift the same flow much higher, to drive it down that long, narrow slope.

scenes.tts: Same flow, different costs. At the same flow, the circuit with more resistance needs the bigger pressure drop. Two separate pumps let each circuit get its own pressure.
scenes.visual: Both halves of the landscape side by side: small lift and short slope on the BLUE side, tall lift and long slope on the RED side, equal flow counters below. A banner draws across: 'At the same flow, the harder circuit costs more pressure.'
scenes.narration: Same flow, different costs. At the same flow, the circuit with more resistance needs the bigger pressure drop. Two separate pumps let each circuit get its own pressure.

scenes.tts: One caution. This rule is bookkeeping on averages over many beats. In a living body, the heart and the vessels set the flow together.
scenes.visual: A small inset trace labelled 'pressure within one beat (schematic)' wobbles up and down; a flat dashed line through it is labelled 'mean'. Beside it, a heart icon and a vessel icon are joined by a two-way arrow labelled 'flow set together'. Tag on the main landscape: 'mean, steady state'.
scenes.narration: One caution. This rule is bookkeeping on averages over many beats. In a living body, the heart and the vessels set the flow together.

scenes.tts: Now a heart with one pump. A teleost fish, such as a trout, has one ventricle. It drives blood through its narrow gill capillaries first, then on to the body.
scenes.visual: Cut to a side-view cartoon trout. Its loop is drawn as one line: a single GOLD lift (labelled 'ventricle'), then a narrow GREY section labelled 'gill capillaries' where BLUE dots turn RED, then a slope labelled 'body', then back to the lift. Same colour map as before.
scenes.narration: Now a heart with one pump. A teleost fish, such as a trout, has one ventricle. It drives blood through its narrow gill capillaries first, then on to the body.

scenes.tts: Here is the question. Blood leaves the gills and reaches the body. Is its pressure the same as the ventricle made, higher, or lower?
scenes.visual: The fish landscape freezes just after the GOLD lift, with the gill narrowing ahead and the body slope beyond it. Three answer cards appear: 'same', 'higher', 'lower'.
scenes.narration: Here is the question. Blood leaves the gills and reaches the body. Is its pressure the same as the ventricle made, higher, or lower?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Cards hold. A 5-second ring timer counts down at bottom right.

scenes.tts: Lower. The gill capillaries resist the flow, so part of the pressure is spent there. The body is supplied with only what is left.
scenes.visual: The card 'lower' glows. Dots roll down a steep drop through the narrow gill section, labelled 'pressure spent in the gills'; they reach the body slope already much lower than the top of the lift, labelled 'what is left for the body'. The body slope continues down to the bottom.
scenes.narration: Lower. The gill capillaries resist the flow, so part of the pressure is spent there. The body is supplied with only what is left.

scenes.tts: Birds and mammals avoid that trade. They have two pumps. The lungs run at low pressure and the body at high pressure. Both carry the full flow.
scenes.visual: Split screen: left, the fish landscape with one lift and the gill drop first; right, the mammal landscape with two lifts, small lift for 'lungs', tall lift for 'body'. Equal flow counters tick under the two mammal lifts.
scenes.narration: Birds and mammals avoid that trade. They have two pumps. The lungs run at low pressure and the body at high pressure. Both carry the full flow.

scenes.tts: One flow, two costs. Both sides move the same blood. The harder circuit, the body's, takes the bigger pressure drop.
scenes.visual: The mammal landscape alone again: two GOLD lifts, BLUE and RED dots streaming round, equal counters ticking. The two pressure drops are highlighted as brackets, small on the lung side and large on the body side.
scenes.narration: One flow, two costs. Both sides move the same blood. The harder circuit, the body's, takes the bigger pressure drop.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Line: 'At the same flow, the harder circuit costs more pressure.'
